entry_json.definition: the fact that you can do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Reading quickly is a useful ability in the IELTS test.
example_sentences: She has the ability to explain hard ideas in simple words.
Children lose the ability to hear new sounds very early.

confusables.difference: An ability is what you are able to do, often something you were born with. A skill is something you learned and practised, like driving or cooking.

entry_json.avoid: Say "the ability to speak", not "the ability of speaking".

entry_json.definition: having what you need in order to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was able to finish the essay before the time ran out.
example_sentences: Are you able to come to class on Friday?
Not everyone is able to study and work at the same time.

confusables.difference: They mean the same, but 'can' has no future or perfect form. Use 'will be able to' and 'have been able to' where 'can' will not work.

entry_json.avoid: After 'able' use 'to' and a verb: "able to swim", never "able swim".

entry_json.definition: on the subject of; or a little more or less than a number
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The talk was about how cities can cut traffic.
example_sentences: We spoke about my plans for next year.
It takes about twenty minutes to walk there.

contexts.text: Tell me about the town where you grew up.
The report is about the cost of public transport.

entry_json.definition: higher than something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The temperature stayed above thirty degrees all week.
example_sentences: My flat is above a small coffee shop.
Scores above seven are treated as strong.

confusables.difference: 'Above' means higher in position or in number, with no touching and no movement. 'Over' can also mean covering or crossing: a bridge goes over a river, not above it.

entry_json.definition: in or to another country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Studying abroad taught me more than any course at home.
example_sentences: My sister works abroad and sends money to my parents.
Have you ever travelled abroad on your own?
entry_json.avoid: Never "go to abroad" or "in abroad". Abroad already contains the idea of 'to' and 'in'.

entry_json.definition: to say yes to something that is offered, or to agree that something is true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I accepted the job because the hours suited my studies.
example_sentences: The university accepted her application in March.
Most people now accept that the climate is changing.

confusables.difference: These sound close but do different work. Accept is a verb: I accept your offer. Except means 'not including': everyone except me.

entry_json.definition: something bad that happens without anyone planning it, often hurting someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was a road accident near the school, so the bus was late.
example_sentences: He broke his arm in a cycling accident.
Better street lighting would prevent many accidents.
entry_json.avoid: We have an accident; we do not 'do' or 'make' an accident.

entry_json.definition: to succeed in doing something after trying hard
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I achieved the band score I needed on my second attempt.
example_sentences: She achieved excellent results in her final exams.
Nothing is achieved without regular practice.

confusables.difference: You reach a place or a level; you achieve a goal or a result. 'Reach my goal' is possible, but 'achieve' is the stronger word in writing.

entry_json.definition: from one side of something to the other side
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We walked across the bridge to reach the old town.
example_sentences: There is a chemist across the road from my house.
The disease spread quickly across the country.

confusables.difference: Across is over a flat surface, like a road or a field. Through is inside something with sides or a roof, like a tunnel, a forest or a crowd.

entry_json.definition: to do something, especially to deal with a problem; also to play a part in a play or film
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Governments need to act now if they want to cut pollution.
example_sentences: The police acted quickly and nobody was hurt.
She has acted in three films this year.

entry_json.definition: the process of doing something in order to change a situation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Talking about waste is easy; taking action is harder.
example_sentences: The council took action after the flood.
Urgent action is needed to protect the forest.
entry_json.avoid: We TAKE action. Never "do action" or "make action".

entry_json.definition: busy doing things, especially moving your body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling to work keeps me active during the week.
example_sentences: My grandmother is still very active at eighty.
He is an active member of the local sports club.

entry_json.definition: something that you do, often for fun or for a purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Swimming is my favourite weekend activity.
example_sentences: The school offers a range of after-school activities.
Outdoor activities are popular with young families.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to play a part in a film, play or television programme
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My favourite actor started out in small theatre roles.
example_sentences: The actor spoke about the training the part required.
Very few actors earn a lot of money.

entry_json.definition: a woman whose job is to play a part in a film, play or television programme
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The actress who played the mother was only twenty-five.
example_sentences: She became a well-known actress in her thirties.
The award for best actress went to a newcomer.

confusables.difference: Many women now prefer 'actor' for both men and women. 'Actress' is still correct and common, but 'actor' is the safer neutral choice.

entry_json.definition: used to say what is really true, often when it is different from what people think
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People say the course is hard, but actually the first year is quite gentle.
example_sentences: I thought it was expensive, but it was actually quite cheap.
Actually, I have never been to the capital.

confusables.difference: In many languages the word that looks like 'actually' means 'now'. In English it does not. For 'now', say currently or at the moment.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'actually' to mean 'at present'. "I actually live in Rome" means "in fact I live in Rome", not "I live there now".

entry_json.definition: to put something with something else to make it bigger or more complete
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I added a short conclusion to make the essay complete.
example_sentences: Add a little salt to the water before it boils.
The new line will add ten stations to the network.

entry_json.definition: a person who has finished growing and is no longer a child
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The class is for adults who work during the day.
example_sentences: Adults pay full price; children under ten go free.
Many adults return to study in their thirties.

entry_json.definition: something that helps you or puts you in a better position
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One advantage of living near campus is that I save on travel.
example_sentences: Speaking two languages is a real advantage at work.
The essay asks for the advantages and disadvantages of online study.

confusables.difference: An advantage is a better position, usually compared with someone or something else. A benefit is a good result that you receive, like better health.

entry_json.avoid: Say "an advantage of doing something" or "the advantage is that...", not "the advantage to do".

entry_json.definition: an exciting experience, often one that could be dangerous
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Travelling alone for the first time felt like a real adventure.
example_sentences: The trip turned into an adventure when the road was closed.
Children need a sense of adventure, not just screens.

entry_json.definition: to tell the public about a product or job so that people will buy it or apply
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The company advertises its courses on social media.
example_sentences: The job was advertised in the local paper.
Firms should not be allowed to advertise junk food to children.

entry_json.definition: a notice, picture or short film that tries to make people buy something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I found my flat through an advertisement on a student website.
example_sentences: There was a full-page advertisement in the newspaper.
Children see hundreds of advertisements every week.

confusables.difference: An advertisement is one single notice or film. Advertising is the whole business or activity, and cannot be counted: "advertising is expensive", but "three advertisements".

entry_json.avoid: In speech people usually say 'advert' or 'ad'. Note the British stress: ad-VER-tis-ment.

entry_json.definition: the business of telling the public about products so that they buy them
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Advertising aimed at young children should be limited.
example_sentences: She works in advertising for a small agency.
Online advertising now earns more than television.
entry_json.avoid: Advertising is uncountable. Not "an advertising" or "advertisings".

entry_json.definition: words that tell someone what you think they should do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My teacher gave me some useful advice about timing the writing task.
example_sentences: Can I ask you for some advice?
The website offers free advice on student visas.

confusables.difference: Advice is the noun and ends in a soft 'ss' sound. Advise is the verb and ends in a 'z' sound: she advised me to wait, and it was good advice.

entry_json.avoid: Advice is uncountable. Not "an advice" or "advices" — say "a piece of advice".

entry_json.definition: to make something change, usually in a way you did not choose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Noise from the road affects my sleep during the week.
example_sentences: The strike affected thousands of passengers.
Long working hours affect family life.

confusables.difference: Affect is the verb, effect is the noun. Pollution affects health; pollution has an effect on health. If you can put 'the' in front of it, you need effect.

entry_json.avoid: Not "affect to" or "affect on". The verb takes a direct object: it affects health.

entry_json.definition: feeling fear; worried that something bad may happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was afraid of speaking English in public until I joined a club.
example_sentences: She is afraid of flying, so she takes the train.
I am afraid I cannot come on Saturday.
entry_json.avoid: 'I'm afraid...' is a polite way to give bad news, and has nothing to do with fear.

entry_json.definition: later than something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After the exam I slept for twelve hours.
example_sentences: I usually study after dinner.
She went back to work after two months.

confusables.difference: After needs something to follow it: after lunch. Afterwards stands alone at the end: we had lunch and went shopping afterwards.

entry_json.avoid: After a time expression use the present for the future: "After I finish, I will call you", not "After I will finish".

entry_json.definition: the part of the day between midday and the evening
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have lectures every Tuesday afternoon.
example_sentences: Shall we meet on Friday afternoon?
The shop closes at two in the afternoon.
entry_json.avoid: Use 'in the afternoon' generally, but 'on Monday afternoon' for a named day.

entry_json.definition: one more time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I read the question again to make sure I had understood it.
example_sentences: Could you say that again, please?
He failed the test but sat it again in June.

entry_json.definition: not agreeing with something, or opposite to it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many residents are against the plan to build on the park.
example_sentences: The team played against the champions and lost.
I have nothing against online lessons, but I prefer class.

confusables.difference: Both show disagreement. 'Against' is everyday and fine in speaking; 'opposed to' is more formal and suits Task 2 writing.

entry_json.definition: how old a person or thing is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children start school at the age of five in my country.
example_sentences: At what age can you drive here?
People are living longer, so the average age is rising.
entry_json.avoid: Say "I am twenty" or "I am twenty years old", never "I have twenty years".

entry_json.definition: before now
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I moved to this city three years ago.
example_sentences: We met a long time ago.
The factory closed ten years ago.

confusables.difference: Ago counts back from now and follows the time: two years ago. Before counts back from a point in the past and comes after it too, but needs that point: two years before the war.

entry_json.avoid: 'Ago' goes with the past simple, never the present perfect. "I have seen him two days ago" is wrong.

entry_json.definition: to think the same as someone else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I agree that public transport should be cheaper.
example_sentences: Do you agree with this statement?
We agreed to meet outside the library.
entry_json.avoid: Agree is a verb on its own: "I agree", not "I am agree". You agree WITH a person and agree TO a plan.

entry_json.definition: a sound people make to show they now understand, or that they feel surprise or pity
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Ah, now I see what the question is asking.
example_sentences: Ah, that explains why the bus was late.
Ah, I'm sorry to hear that.
entry_json.avoid: This belongs in speech only. Never write it in an IELTS essay.

entry_json.definition: the gas all around us that we breathe
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The air in my home city is much cleaner than it was ten years ago.
example_sentences: Cyclists breathe in dirty air on busy roads.
I opened the window to let some fresh air in.
entry_json.avoid: Air is uncountable: not "airs".

entry_json.definition: a company that carries people and things by plane
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The airline lost my bag on the way to the conference.
example_sentences: Budget airlines have made flying much cheaper.
The airline offers three flights a day to Dubai.

entry_json.definition: a place where planes land and take off, with buildings for passengers
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The airport is forty minutes from the city by train.
example_sentences: I got to the airport two hours early.
A second airport would bring jobs but also noise.

entry_json.definition: living, not dead
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My great-grandmother is still alive and nearly a hundred.
example_sentences: The fish were still alive in the tank.
Traditional music is very much alive in the villages.

confusables.difference: 'Alive' comes after the verb: he is alive. 'Living' can come before a noun: a living language. We do not say "an alive man".

entry_json.avoid: Never put 'alive' before a noun.

entry_json.definition: the whole of something, or every one of a group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: All the students in my group passed the first test.
example_sentences: I spent all day in the library.
All of my friends use the same app.
entry_json.avoid: Before 'the', 'my' or 'these' you may use 'all' or 'all of': all the students, all of the students. Before a pronoun you need 'of': all of us.

entry_json.definition: to let someone do something, or to say that it is possible
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My university allows students to take one year out.
example_sentences: Smoking is not allowed anywhere in the building.
Flexible hours allow parents to collect their children.

confusables.difference: They mean the same, but the grammar differs. 'Let' takes no 'to': let me go. 'Allow' needs 'to': allow me to go. 'Let' is more spoken.

entry_json.avoid: Say "allow someone to do something". Not "allow to do" with no person.

entry_json.definition: very nearly, but not completely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Almost half of my class travel to college by bus.
example_sentences: I have almost finished the report.
It took almost three hours to get there.

confusables.difference: In most sentences they are the same. Only 'almost' can be used with 'no', 'nobody' or 'never': almost never, but not 'nearly never'.

entry_json.avoid: Say "almost all of the students" or "almost every student", not "almost of the students".

entry_json.definition: from one end of something long towards the other, or in a line beside it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We walked along the river until we reached the market.
example_sentences: There are new cycle lanes along the main road.
Shops have opened all along the seafront.

confusables.difference: These look similar but are unrelated. Along is a direction; alone means with nobody else.

entry_json.definition: before now, or sooner than expected
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had already booked my test before the fee went up.
example_sentences: She has already sent the application.
It is only ten o'clock and I am already tired.

confusables.difference: Already is for things that have happened, usually in a positive sentence. Yet is for things that have not happened, in questions and negatives: Have you finished yet? I haven't finished yet.
Still means something continues: I am still waiting. Already means it is finished: I have already waited.

entry_json.definition: in addition; as well
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The course is cheap, and it is also close to my home.
example_sentences: She speaks French and also some Arabic.
Cycling saves money. It also keeps you fit.

confusables.difference: They mean the same, but 'also' goes in the middle of the sentence and 'too' goes at the end: I also went / I went too.

entry_json.avoid: Put 'also' before the main verb but after 'be': she also works, she is also busy.

entry_json.definition: another thing you could choose instead
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling is a cheap alternative to driving in a crowded city.
example_sentences: Is there an alternative to raising the fees?
Solar power is a clean alternative to coal.
entry_json.avoid: Say "an alternative TO something", not "an alternative of".

entry_json.definition: used to join two ideas when the second one is surprising after the first
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Although the course was expensive, it was worth every penny.
example_sentences: Although I studied hard, I did not get the score I wanted.
The city is busy, although it is quiet at weekends.

confusables.difference: Both show contrast, but the grammar differs. 'Although' joins two clauses in one sentence. 'However' starts a new sentence and takes a comma: It was expensive. However, it was worth it.
'Although' is followed by a subject and verb; 'despite' is followed by a noun or -ing: although it rained / despite the rain.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'but' in the same sentence. "Although it was late, but I stayed" is wrong; drop the 'but'.

entry_json.definition: every time, or all the time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I always check my answers before the time is up.
example_sentences: The train is always crowded at eight in the morning.
She has always wanted to work in medicine.
entry_json.avoid: 'Always' goes before the main verb but after 'be': I always walk; I am always late.

entry_json.definition: very surprising and very good
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The view from the top of the hill was amazing.
example_sentences: She made amazing progress in six months.
It is amazing how quickly children pick up a language.

confusables.difference: 'Amazing' describes the thing that causes the feeling; 'amazed' describes the person who has it. The view was amazing, so I was amazed.

entry_json.avoid: 'Amazing' is strong and informal. In Task 2 writing, prefer 'remarkable' or 'impressive'.

entry_json.definition: in the middle of a group of people or things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling is popular among students who live near campus.
example_sentences: The book is among the most borrowed in the library.
Stress is common among first-year students.

confusables.difference: Use 'between' for two things, or for separate things you can name: between London and Paris. Use 'among' for a group you do not count: among the trees, among students.

entry_json.definition: how much of something there is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The amount of plastic in the sea has risen sharply.
example_sentences: A small amount of exercise each day makes a difference.
Students spend a huge amount of time online.

confusables.difference: Use 'amount' with things you cannot count: the amount of water, of time, of money. Use 'number' with things you can count: the number of cars, of students.

entry_json.avoid: Never "the amount of people". People can be counted, so use 'the number of people'.

entry_json.definition: belonging to a time very long ago
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city is famous for its ancient walls.
example_sentences: We visited an ancient temple in the north of the country.
Ancient Rome had a system of public baths.

confusables.difference: 'Ancient' means thousands of years old, or from a lost world. A phone from 2010 is old, not ancient — except as a joke.

entry_json.definition: used to join two words or two ideas together
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I study in the morning and work in the afternoon.
example_sentences: We visited the museum and the old market.
It was cold and wet all week.
entry_json.avoid: In writing, do not start every sentence with 'and'. Use 'in addition' or 'moreover' instead.

entry_json.definition: having a strong bad feeling because something is wrong or not fair
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Local people were angry about the plan to close the library.
example_sentences: He gets angry when the trains are cancelled.
She was angry with me for arriving so late.
entry_json.avoid: Angry WITH a person, angry ABOUT a thing.

entry_json.definition: a living thing that can move, such as a dog, a bird or a fish
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Zoos protect some animals but keep others in small cages.
example_sentences: Wild animals are losing their homes as forests are cut down.
She has loved animals since she was a child.

entry_json.definition: the part of your body where your foot joins your leg
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I hurt my ankle playing football and could not run for a month.
example_sentences: She twisted her ankle on the stairs.
The water was only up to my ankles.

entry_json.definition: something you say or write when someone asks you a question
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I changed my answer at the last minute and got it wrong.
example_sentences: Write your answers on the sheet, not in the booklet.
There is no simple answer to this problem.
entry_json.avoid: Say "the answer TO the question", not "the answer of".

entry_json.definition: used to mean some, when it does not matter which one, or none at all
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I did not have any trouble finding the exam centre.
example_sentences: Is there any milk left?
You can come at any time before six.

confusables.difference: Use 'some' in positive sentences and in offers: I have some money. Use 'any' in negatives and most questions: I don't have any money.

entry_json.definition: any person; it does not matter who
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Anybody can join the club, whatever their level.
example_sentences: I did not tell anybody about the interview.
Does anybody know when the results come out?

confusables.difference: They mean exactly the same. 'Anyone' is a little more common in writing.

entry_json.avoid: 'Anybody' is singular: "Does anybody know?", not "Do anybody know?"

entry_json.definition: any person; it does not matter who
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Anyone who works hard can improve their score.
example_sentences: I have not spoken to anyone about it yet.
Anyone over sixty travels free.

entry_json.definition: any thing; it does not matter what
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I did not eat anything before the test and I regretted it.
example_sentences: Is there anything I can do to help?
You can write about anything you like.

entry_json.definition: used to return to an earlier subject, or to say that something happens whatever else is true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was raining, but we walked there anyway.
example_sentences: Anyway, as I was saying, the course starts in October.
I did not want to go, and I was busy anyway.
entry_json.avoid: This is a speaking word. Avoid it in Task 1 and Task 2 writing.

entry_json.definition: in or to any place; it does not matter where
entry_json.own_context_sentence: With good internet you can study almost anywhere.
example_sentences: I could not find my keys anywhere.
We can meet anywhere near the station.

entry_json.definition: a set of rooms to live in, inside a larger building
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I share a small apartment with two other students.
example_sentences: Their apartment is on the fifth floor.
Apartments near the centre have become very expensive.

confusables.difference: They mean the same thing. British speakers say 'flat'; 'apartment' is American, though it is understood everywhere and used in adverts.

entry_json.definition: a small program you use on a phone or tablet
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I use a free app to test myself on new words every morning.
example_sentences: Which app do you use to plan your journeys?
Banking apps have replaced most trips to the bank.

entry_json.definition: to start to be seen, or to seem to be true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cracks appeared in the wall after the building work next door.
example_sentences: A message appeared on the screen.
She appears to be enjoying the course.

confusables.difference: When it means 'give an impression', 'appear' is the more formal of the two and fits written English better than 'seem'.

entry_json.definition: the way somebody or something looks
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People judge others by their appearance far too quickly.
example_sentences: The new paint has improved the appearance of the building.
Young people spend a lot of money on their appearance.

entry_json.definition: a hard round fruit with red or green skin
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I take an apple with me to eat between lectures.
example_sentences: This region is famous for its apples.
She had toast and an apple for breakfast.

entry_json.definition: to ask for a job, a place at a college or permission, usually in writing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I applied to four universities and was offered two places.
example_sentences: She applied for a part-time job at the library.
You must apply for the visa at least a month early.
entry_json.avoid: Apply FOR a job or a visa; apply TO an organisation. Not "apply a job".

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to design buildings
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My cousin trained as an architect and now designs schools.
example_sentences: The architect showed us the plans for the new library.
Architects are now asked to design greener buildings.
entry_json.avoid: The 'ch' sounds like a 'k'.

entry_json.definition: the art of designing buildings, or the style of the buildings in a place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The old town is known for its wooden architecture.
example_sentences: She is studying architecture in Milan.
Modern architecture does not always suit an old city.
entry_json.avoid: Architecture is uncountable when it means the style or the subject: not "architectures".

entry_json.definition: a part of a town, a country or a space
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I grew up in a quiet area on the edge of the city.
example_sentences: This area has changed a lot in ten years.
Rural areas often lack good public transport.

confusables.difference: An area can be small, even a corner of a room. A region is large: several towns or a whole part of a country.

entry_json.definition: to speak angrily with someone who disagrees with you; or to give reasons for an opinion
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Some people argue that university should be free for everyone.
example_sentences: My brothers argue about money all the time.
The writer argues that cities should ban cars.
entry_json.avoid: In essays, use 'argue that' plus a clause. It is a strong, useful verb for reporting an opinion.

entry_json.definition: an angry disagreement; or a reason given to support an opinion
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a strong argument for making public transport free.
example_sentences: We had an argument about who should pay.
Both arguments are convincing, but I prefer the first.

confusables.difference: An argument is usually angry, or it is a point in an essay. A discussion is calm and between people who want to understand each other.

entry_json.definition: the part of your body from your shoulder to your hand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I broke my arm falling off my bike last winter.
example_sentences: He was carrying a heavy box under one arm.
She folded her arms and waited.

entry_json.definition: the soldiers who fight for a country on land
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandfather served in the army for twenty years.
example_sentences: He joined the army at eighteen.
The army was sent in after the earthquake.

entry_json.definition: on all sides of something; or a little more or a little less, when talking about a number
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are good cafes all around the university.
example_sentences: We walked around the lake in an hour.
Around forty per cent of students live at home.

confusables.difference: When they mean 'roughly', they are the same: about ten / around ten. Only 'around' means 'on all sides'.

entry_json.definition: to plan or organise something so that it will happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I arranged to meet my tutor before the deadline.
example_sentences: The college arranges trips every term.
Can we arrange a time to talk on Friday?

entry_json.definition: a plan you have made with someone for something to happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We made an arrangement to share the cost of the flat.
example_sentences: I have already made arrangements for the weekend.
The new arrangement suits both sides.

entry_json.definition: to get to a place at the end of a journey
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I arrived at the test centre half an hour early.
example_sentences: The train arrives in Manchester at nine.
She arrived home very late last night.

confusables.difference: 'Reach' takes the place directly: reach the airport. 'Arrive' needs a preposition: arrive at the airport.

entry_json.avoid: Arrive IN a city or country, arrive AT a building or a smaller place, and no preposition at all before home: arrive home.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to help someone else at work

entry_json.definition: a person who writes a book or an article

entry_json.definition: the season between summer and winter, when leaves fall

entry_json.definition: able to be used or bought; or free to meet someone

entry_json.definition: to stay away from something, or to try not to do something

entry_json.definition: a prize given to someone for something good they have done

entry_json.definition: to or at a distance from a place or a person

entry_json.definition: a large number of people together in one place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A crowd had already formed outside the hall an hour before the doors opened.
example_sentences: The crowd cheered when the team came out.
She hates crowds, so she shops early.

entry_json.definition: full of people, with little space
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The train is so crowded at eight that I now leave at seven.
example_sentences: The beach was crowded all weekend.
Crowded housing makes it hard for children to study.

confusables.difference: 'Crowd' is the noun, the people themselves. 'Crowded' is the adjective describing the place: a crowd of people, a crowded room.

entry_json.definition: to produce tears from your eyes because you feel sad or hurt
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I nearly cried when I opened the results, out of relief rather than sadness.
example_sentences: The baby cried all night.
She cried when she said goodbye at the airport.
entry_json.avoid: The past is 'cried'.

entry_json.definition: the way of life of a group of people, and the things they do and believe
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Living abroad taught me more about my own culture than about the new one.
example_sentences: Food is an important part of any culture.
The museum celebrates local culture and history.

entry_json.definition: a small round thing that you drink tea or coffee from, with a part at the side to hold it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A cup of tea is how every difficult conversation starts in this country.
example_sentences: Would you like a cup of coffee?
She washed the cups and left them to dry.

confusables.difference: A cup is for hot drinks and has a handle. A glass is clear, has no handle and is for cold drinks.

entry_json.definition: a piece of furniture with doors and shelves, used for storing things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a cupboard in the hall where we keep everything we never use.
example_sentences: The plates are in the cupboard above the sink.
She keeps her books in a cupboard.
entry_json.avoid: The 'p' is silent and it has two syllables: KUB-əd.

entry_json.definition: with hair or lines that turn in rings, not straight
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My sister has curly hair and mine is completely straight.
example_sentences: He has short curly hair.
The photo shows a small child with curly brown hair.

entry_json.definition: a person who buys something from a shop or a business
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The cafe keeps its regular customers because the staff never change.
example_sentences: The shop was full of customers on Saturday.
Good customer service costs money but keeps people coming back.

confusables.difference: A customer buys goods in a shop. A client pays for a professional service, from a lawyer, designer or accountant.

entry_json.definition: to use a knife to make something into pieces or to make a hole in it; or to make an amount smaller
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council plans to cut spending on street cleaning.
example_sentences: Cut the vegetables into small pieces.
The company cut prices by ten per cent.
entry_json.avoid: The past tense and past participle are also 'cut': I cut it yesterday.

entry_json.definition: to travel by bicycle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cycle to work whenever the weather allows.
example_sentences: She cycles ten kilometres each way.
More people would cycle if the lanes were separated from traffic.
entry_json.avoid: 'Cycle' is the normal British verb; Americans usually say 'ride a bike'.

entry_json.definition: an informal word for father
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My dad taught me to drive in an empty car park on Sunday mornings.
example_sentences: My dad works nights at the hospital.
I called my dad from the airport.

confusables.difference: 'Dad' is what you call him and what you say to friends. 'Father' is formal and belongs in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'dad' in an IELTS essay; use 'father' or 'parents'.

entry_json.definition: happening every day
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A short daily walk did more for my health than the gym membership I never used.
example_sentences: The daily commute takes over an hour.
She reads a daily newspaper on the train.

entry_json.definition: to move your body in time with music
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At the festival everyone danced in the street until well after midnight.
example_sentences: We danced for hours at the wedding.
She learned to dance as a child.

entry_json.definition: a person who dances, especially as a job
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The dancers had trained together since they were children.
example_sentences: She is a professional dancer with a small company.
He is a good dancer but says he is not.

entry_json.definition: the activity of moving to music
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Dancing is the cheapest exercise I know and the only one I enjoy.
example_sentences: We go dancing every Friday night.
Dancing lessons start at seven.
entry_json.avoid: We GO dancing, as with 'go swimming' and 'go shopping'.

entry_json.definition: the chance that something bad will happen and hurt you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The real danger of studying alone is that nobody corrects your mistakes.
example_sentences: There is a danger that the river will flood again.
Children were in danger from the traffic outside the school.
entry_json.avoid: Say "in danger", not 'in the danger'.

entry_json.definition: not safe, because it can hurt someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling here is only dangerous where the lanes stop suddenly.
example_sentences: It is dangerous to swim beyond the flags.
Working at night on the roads is dangerous.
entry_json.avoid: Say "it is dangerous TO do something".

entry_json.definition: with little or no light; or close to black in colour
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It gets dark here at four in the afternoon in December.
example_sentences: She was wearing a dark blue suit.
Do not walk home through the park after dark.
entry_json.avoid: Use 'it' for light: "it is dark", not "there is dark".

entry_json.definition: facts and numbers collected so they can be studied
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The data show a steady fall in car use among people under thirty.
example_sentences: We collected data from four hundred students.
The data is stored on a secure server.

confusables.difference: 'Information' is always uncountable. 'Data' is usually treated as uncountable too in everyday use, but scientific writing often takes a plural verb: the data show.

entry_json.avoid: Never "datas". Both "the data is" and "the data are" are accepted; be consistent.

entry_json.definition: a particular day of a month or year
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Write the date at the top of the form.
example_sentences: What is the date of your test?
The closing date for applications is 3 May.
entry_json.avoid: Say "on 3 May" or "on the third of May".

entry_json.definition: a person's female child
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Their daughter has just started at the same school I went to.
example_sentences: She has a daughter and two sons.
His daughter is studying abroad.
entry_json.avoid: The 'gh' is silent: DAW-tə.

entry_json.definition: a period of twenty-four hours, or the time when it is light
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I study best in the first two hours of the day.
example_sentences: It rained every day for a fortnight.
The museum is open six days a week.

confusables.difference: 'Every day' as two words means daily: I walk every day. 'Everyday' as one word is an adjective: everyday clothes.

entry_json.definition: no longer alive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The tree at the front of the house has been dead for two winters.
example_sentences: My grandfather has been dead for ten years.
The battery in the smoke alarm was dead.

confusables.difference: 'Dead' is an adjective describing a state: he is dead. 'Died' is the past of the verb: he died in 2010. "He is died" is wrong.

entry_json.avoid: Never "he is died" or "he has dead".

entry_json.definition: when two people or companies agree to do something together, especially in business; or a large amount when used with 'great'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We got a good deal on the flat because the last tenant left in a hurry.
example_sentences: The two companies signed a deal last week.
A great deal of money was spent on the road.
entry_json.avoid: 'A great deal of' is used with uncountable nouns: a great deal of time, not "a great deal of people".

entry_json.definition: used at the start of a letter or email before a person's name
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Dear Sir or Madam is still the safest opening when you do not have a name.
example_sentences: Dear Ms Ahmed, I am writing to ask about the course.
Dear Tom, thanks for sending the notes.
entry_json.avoid: In a formal letter, 'Dear Sir or Madam' pairs with 'Yours faithfully'; 'Dear Mr Smith' pairs with 'Yours sincerely'.

entry_json.definition: the end of life
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air pollution causes thousands of early deaths every year.
example_sentences: The number of deaths on the roads has fallen.
After his death the house was sold.

confusables.difference: 'Death' is the noun, the event. 'Dead' is the adjective, the state. "After his dead" is wrong — say "after his death".

entry_json.definition: to choose what you will do after thinking about it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I decided to take the test in June rather than wait until autumn.
example_sentences: We decided against buying a car.
She has not decided which course to apply for.
entry_json.avoid: Say "decide TO do something", never "decide doing".

entry_json.definition: a choice you make after thinking
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Moving here was the best decision I have made.
example_sentences: The council made its decision last night.
It was a difficult decision to leave my job.
entry_json.avoid: We MAKE a decision, never 'take' one in the American sense and never 'do' one.

entry_json.definition: going a long way down from the top
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The river is deep enough for ships as far as the old bridge.
example_sentences: The water is too deep for children here.
She took a deep breath before she started.
entry_json.avoid: The measurement goes before the word: "two metres deep".

entry_json.definition: for sure; used when you are completely sure about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I will definitely apply again if I do not get the score I need.
example_sentences: That is definitely the right answer.
She is definitely coming to the meeting.
entry_json.avoid: The spelling has no 'a': definitely, not "definately". This is one of the most common written errors in English.

entry_json.definition: the title you get when you finish a course at university; or a unit for how hot something is or how big a turn is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A degree opens the first door, but experience opens the rest.
example_sentences: She has a degree in economics.
The temperature reached thirty-five degrees.
entry_json.avoid: Say "a degree IN economics", not "a degree of economics".

entry_json.definition: tasting very good
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The soup at the market stall is cheap and delicious.
example_sentences: That cake was delicious, thank you.
Street food here is delicious and safe.
entry_json.avoid: 'Delicious' is already strong, so avoid 'very delicious'. Use 'absolutely delicious' instead.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to look after people's teeth
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I go to the dentist twice a year, whether anything hurts or not.
example_sentences: I have an appointment at the dentist on Thursday.
The dentist said I should use a softer brush.
entry_json.avoid: Use 'the': "go to the dentist".

entry_json.definition: one part of a large organisation such as a university, shop or government
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The engineering department has its own library on the top floor.
example_sentences: She works in the sales department.
The health department published new guidance.
entry_json.avoid: You work IN a department.

entry_json.definition: to be affected or decided by something else; or to need someone for help
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How long the journey takes depends on the traffic.
example_sentences: Whether I apply depends on the fee.
Many older people depend on the bus service.
entry_json.avoid: Always 'depend ON'. "It depends of the weather" and "depends to" are both wrong.

entry_json.definition: to say what someone or something is like
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In Part 2 you are asked to describe a place that matters to you.
example_sentences: Describe the chart in your own words.
She described the flat as small but bright.
entry_json.avoid: Never "describe me the picture". Say "describe the picture to me".

entry_json.definition: words that say what someone or something is like
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The description of the flat online left out the noise from the road.
example_sentences: Give a full description of what happened.
The job description lists eight main duties.
entry_json.avoid: Say "a description OF something".

entry_json.definition: a large dry area of land with very little rain, where few plants can grow
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Parts of the region are turning into desert as the rains fail.
example_sentences: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world.
Very few plants survive in the desert.

confusables.difference: One 's' and stress on the first syllable is the dry land: DEZ-ət. Two 's's and stress on the second is the sweet course after a meal: dih-ZERT.

entry_json.definition: the way something is planned and made, or a drawing showing this
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Good design makes a small flat feel twice the size.
example_sentences: The design of the new station won an award.
She studies graphic design.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to decide how something will look and work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The designer had clearly never carried a pram up those steps.
example_sentences: She works as a web designer.
The designer chose local wood for the whole building.

entry_json.definition: a table you sit at to write or work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cleared my desk completely before I started revising.
example_sentences: There is a lamp on my desk.
Ask at the information desk on the ground floor.
entry_json.avoid: We sit AT a desk.

entry_json.definition: to break something so badly that it is gone or cannot be fixed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fire destroyed three shops in the old market.
example_sentences: The forest was destroyed to make room for farmland.
War destroyed most of the city centre.

confusables.difference: 'Damage' means harmed but still there and possibly repairable. 'Destroy' means gone for good.

entry_json.definition: a small fact or piece of information about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The examiner wants detail, not just a general answer.
example_sentences: She explained the plan in detail.
Please check the details on your ticket.
entry_json.avoid: The fixed phrase is 'in detail', with no article and no plural.

entry_json.definition: a police officer or other person whose job is to find out who broke the law
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Detective stories are good practice because you keep reading to find out what happened.
example_sentences: A detective interviewed all the neighbours.
She reads a detective novel a week.

entry_json.definition: to grow or change into something bigger or better, or to make something new over time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took a year of daily practice to develop any real confidence in speaking.
example_sentences: The company is developing a cheaper battery.
The town has developed quickly since the road was built.
entry_json.avoid: No double p in the base form: develop, but developed and developing.

entry_json.definition: a piece of equipment made for a particular purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most students now do their reading on a device rather than on paper.
example_sentences: The hospital uses a small device to measure blood sugar.
Turn off all electronic devices during the test.
entry_json.avoid: 'Device' is the noun; 'devise' is the verb meaning to invent, and sounds different at the end.

entry_json.definition: a conversation between two people, especially in a book, play or lesson
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We practised a short dialogue about booking a room.
example_sentences: Listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.
The two governments have begun a dialogue about trade.
entry_json.avoid: British spelling keeps the 'ue': dialogue. American English often writes 'dialog'.

entry_json.definition: a book where you write what you do each day, or plan what you will do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I keep a diary in English, which forces me to write something every night.
example_sentences: Let me check my diary for Thursday.
She has kept a diary since she was twelve.

confusables.difference: These two look alike but are unrelated. A diary is a book; dairy means milk products, and the vowels are in the other order.

entry_json.definition: a book or app that lists words and explains what they mean
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Use a dictionary that explains words in English, not one that only translates.
example_sentences: Look the word up in a dictionary.
A learner's dictionary gives example sentences too.
entry_json.avoid: We look a word UP IN a dictionary.

entry_json.definition: to stop living
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandmother died at ninety-one, in the house she was born in.
example_sentences: Thousands of trees died in the drought.
He died two years before I was born.

confusables.difference: 'Die' is the verb: he died last year. 'Dead' is the adjective: he is dead. Do not mix them.

entry_json.avoid: The -ing form is 'dying', with a y. 'Dyeing' with an e means colouring cloth.

entry_json.definition: the food a person or group usually eats
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A diet with more vegetables and less meat is better for you and for the planet.
example_sentences: She is on a diet before the wedding.
A balanced diet matters more than any single food.
entry_json.avoid: 'Your diet' is what you normally eat; 'on a diet' means eating less to lose weight. The two senses are different.

entry_json.definition: the way in which two things are not the same
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main difference between the two courses is the number of contact hours.
example_sentences: There is a big difference between reading and speaking.
Ten minutes of planning makes a real difference to an essay.
entry_json.avoid: Say "the difference BETWEEN A and B", not "the difference of".

entry_json.definition: not the same as something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Life in a small town is completely different from life in the capital.
example_sentences: The two reports reach different conclusions.
She is very different from her sister.
entry_json.avoid: British English prefers 'different from'; 'different to' is also accepted, but 'different than' sounds American.

entry_json.definition: in a way that is not the same
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People learn differently, so one method will never suit everyone.
example_sentences: The word is pronounced differently in the north.
She sees the problem differently from me.

entry_json.definition: not easy to do or understand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The listening test is difficult mainly because you hear it only once.
example_sentences: It is difficult to find a cheap flat near the centre.
She asked a difficult question.

confusables.difference: They mean the same here, but 'hard' also means solid, and 'difficult' can describe a person who is not easy to deal with.

entry_json.avoid: Say "it is difficult TO do something" or "I find it difficult to", not "I am difficult to".

entry_json.definition: using information stored as numbers in a computer
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Older people can be left behind as services move to digital only.
example_sentences: The library has a large digital collection.
Digital skills are now needed for almost every job.
